UNIV 497: Interdisciplinary Capstone Studio
Fall 2026 | Instructor: Dr. Renata Okafor | Project Brief and Course Policies
1. Course overview
In this capstone, interdisciplinary teams of four to six students partner with a community sponsor to research,
design, prototype, and test a solution to a real problem the sponsor faces. You will work the way professional
project teams work: you will scope the problem with your sponsor, research the people affected, build and test a
prototype, and present a recommendation. No single major is expected to carry the project. Every team needs
research, design, technical, writing, and client-management skills, and the grading reflects that.
The semester runs 15 instructional weeks. Week 1 begins Monday, August 24, 2026. Thanksgiving break
(November 23 to 29) is not a course week. Week 14 begins Monday, November 30, and Week 15 begins
Monday, December 7.
2. Deliverables and due dates
All written deliverables are submitted on the course site by 11:59 pm on the due date unless noted.

3. Grading summary
Team milestones (M0 through M5) account for 90% of the course grade and are scored as a team. The
remaining 10% is individual and is based on peer evaluations, the contribution logs described in Section 5, and
instructor observation. A student whose contribution is documented as substantially below the team's may
receive an individually adjusted milestone grade. This is rare and is always preceded by a conversation with the
instructor.
4. Milestone 3: Prototype and sponsor demo (20%)
Milestone 3 shows that your team can turn its research into something the sponsor can see and react to. The
prototype may be coded or built in a design tool (for example, a clickable prototype) as long as a person can
complete each core user flow without help. The sponsor demo must take place during Week 10, no later than
Thursday, October 29, so that sponsor feedback can be included in the submission.

Required with every milestone submission: a contribution log (see Section 5). A missing log costs five points

Milestones 4 and 5 (summary)
M4 requires a usability test with at least five participants from the sponsor's actual user group, a findings
summary, and the changes made in response. M5 requires a 15-minute final presentation to the class and
sponsor, and a final report covering the problem, research, solution, test results, implementation
recommendations, and limitations. Detailed rubrics for M4 and M5 will be posted by Week 11.
5. Course policies
Late work. Team milestones lose 10% per calendar day late, up to three days. After three days, the milestone
receives no credit unless an extension was approved.
Extensions. Extension requests must reach the instructor at least 48 hours before the deadline and must
explain the cause and the proposed new date. Extensions for sponsor scheduling conflicts are considered case
by case.
Sponsor communication. Each team names one sponsor liaison, but every team member is responsible for
professional conduct with the sponsor. Copy the instructor on all email to the sponsor. Sponsors are volunteers
with full-time jobs: sponsor meetings and demos must be requested from the sponsor at least seven
calendar days before the proposed date.
Contribution log. Each milestone submission includes a short table listing what each team member
contributed since the previous milestone. Include work that does not show up in a task tracker, such as design
iterations, sponsor communication, editing, and coordination.
Peer evaluation. Each student completes a confidential peer evaluation form, due on the same date as M3 and
again with M5. Peer evaluations are read only by the instructor.
Team concerns. Teams are expected to talk through workload and communication problems among
themselves first, using the conflict plan in their charter. If that does not resolve a concern, any team member
may contact the instructor. Concerns raised by the end of Week 10 (Friday, Oct 30) can be addressed before
final grading; concerns raised only at the end of the semester are much harder to act on.

Accommodations. Students with work, caregiving, commuting, or disability-related constraints are encouraged
to share what they are comfortable sharing with their team when the charter is written, so the team can plan
around it. Students may also speak with the instructor privately.
AI use. AI tools may be used for drafting, analysis, and prototyping. Note in each submission where AI tools
were used. Do not enter sponsor data or interview recordings into AI tools without the sponsor's permission.

Team 4 project description
Palouse Harvest Food Share relies on about 140 active volunteers to staff food sorting, distribution days, and
deliveries. Volunteers currently sign up through a mix of a paper sheet at the warehouse, a shared online form,
and text messages to the volunteer coordinator. Shifts are regularly under-staffed or double-booked, and the
coordinator spends several hours a week confirming who is coming.
The sponsor has asked the team to design a solution in which:
• volunteers can see open shifts and sign up from a phone;
• volunteers receive a reminder before each shift; and
• the coordinator can see who is scheduled for each shift and day.
The sponsor has also mentioned interest in a way for volunteers to see a record of their hours. The team should
confirm the priority of this and any other requests with the sponsor and document the agreed scope in M1. The
solution does not need to be production software; the sponsor's goal is a tested design and a recommendation
they can take to a volunteer developer or vendor.
